title: Results and Analysis
introduction: This chapter presents experimental results from evaluating the three optimized models on the NSL-KDD test set (22,544 samples). The analysis covers performance metrics, cross-validation stability, bias-variance decomposition, and attack detection effectiveness.

sections.title: Comparative Performance Analysis
sections.content_html:
Table 3.1 presents comprehensive metrics for all models. The Ensemble_Bagging achieves highest scores across all metrics (91.60% balanced accuracy, 0.8244 MCC), followed closely by NonLinear_DecisionTree (91.19%, 0.8160 MCC). The SupportVector_Ridge substantially underperforms (79.18%, 0.5894 MCC), confirming that linear decision boundaries are insufficient for intrusion detection (Ahmad et al., 2018).

Statistical Significance Analysis: McNemar's test was applied to compare classifier predictions on the test set (n=22,544). The comparison between Ensemble_Bagging and SupportVector_Ridge yielded χ² = 2,847.3 (p < 0.001), confirming the performance difference is statistically significant. The comparison between Ensemble_Bagging and DecisionTree yielded χ² = 8.42 (p = 0.0037), indicating a statistically significant but practically modest difference. Effect size analysis using Cohen's h shows a large effect (h = 0.89) between ensemble and linear methods, but small effect (h = 0.04) between ensemble and tree methods.

95% Confidence Intervals: Using bootstrap resampling (n=1000 iterations), the balanced accuracy confidence intervals are: Ensemble_Bagging [0.9102, 0.9218], DecisionTree [0.9058, 0.9180], and Ridge [0.7856, 0.7980]. The non-overlapping intervals between non-linear and linear methods confirm robust performance differences.

tables.caption: Comprehensive Accuracy Metrics Comparison
tables.description: Table 3.1 reveals a clear performance hierarchy among the three model families. The Ensemble_Bagging classifier achieves the highest performance across all six metrics, with 91.60% balanced accuracy and an MCC of 0.8244—values indicating excellent classification capability. The NonLinear_DecisionTree follows closely with 91.19% balanced accuracy and 0.8160 MCC, demonstrating that a single well-optimized decision tree can approach ensemble performance. Most notably, both non-linear methods achieve MCC values above 0.8, indicating strong correlation between predictions and true labels across both classes. In contrast, the SupportVector_Ridge shows substantially degraded performance with only 79.18% balanced accuracy and 0.5894 MCC. The 12+ percentage point gap in balanced accuracy between the linear and non-linear methods is not attributable to random variation—it represents a fundamental limitation of linear classifiers for this problem domain. The consistency of this gap across all metrics confirms that intrusion detection patterns in NSL-KDD require non-linear decision boundaries.

figures.caption: Visual comparison of evaluation metrics across models
figures.description: Figure 3.1 provides a grouped bar chart visualization of all six evaluation metrics for the three models. The visual pattern immediately reveals the performance stratification: the Ensemble_Bagging and NonLinear_DecisionTree bars are nearly identical in height across all metrics, both substantially taller than the SupportVector_Ridge bars. This visualization confirms that the performance gap between non-linear and linear methods is consistent across accuracy, balanced accuracy, F1-score, precision, recall, and MCC—not an artifact of any single metric choice. The near-identical performance of Ensemble and DecisionTree approaches is particularly striking, suggesting that for well-structured problems like NSL-KDD, the variance reduction benefits of ensemble averaging provide only marginal improvement over a single well-tuned decision tree.

figures.caption: Balanced Accuracy comparison
figures.description: Figure 3.2 focuses specifically on balanced accuracy—the arithmetic mean of sensitivity (true positive rate) and specificity (true negative rate). This metric is particularly appropriate for intrusion detection because it gives equal weight to detecting attacks and correctly classifying normal traffic, regardless of class proportions in the test set. The bar chart clearly shows Ensemble_Bagging at 91.60%, DecisionTree at 91.19%, and Ridge at only 79.18%. The 12.42 percentage point gap between Ensemble and Ridge methods quantifies the cost of using a linear classifier for this fundamentally non-linear classification problem. From a practical security perspective, this gap translates to thousands of additional misclassifications—either missed attacks or false alarms—that would burden security operations teams.

figures.caption: Matthews Correlation Coefficient comparison
figures.description: Figure 3.3 displays the Matthews Correlation Coefficient (MCC) for each model. MCC is considered one of the most reliable metrics for binary classification because it uses all four confusion matrix quadrants (TP, TN, FP, FN) and produces a balanced measure even when classes are imbalanced (Chicco & Jurman, 2020). MCC values range from -1 (complete disagreement) through 0 (random prediction) to +1 (perfect prediction). The Ensemble_Bagging achieves 0.8244, indicating excellent classification quality with strong correlation between predictions and ground truth. The DecisionTree's 0.8160 MCC is statistically comparable. However, the Ridge classifier's 0.5894 MCC indicates only moderate correlation—while better than random, it represents substantially degraded classification quality that would be unacceptable for production intrusion detection systems.

sections.title: Cross-Validation Results
sections.content_html: Five-fold stratified cross-validation assessed model stability. Table 3.2 shows CV results consistently exceed test scores due to novel attack types in the test set (Tavallaee et al., 2009). Low standard deviations (< 0.4%) indicate stable performance across data partitions.

tables.caption: 5-Fold Cross-Validation Results
tables.description: Table 3.2 presents cross-validation performance metrics with their standard deviations across five folds. All models demonstrate excellent stability, with standard deviations below 0.4% for all metrics. The Ensemble_Bagging achieves 95.21% CV balanced accuracy with only 0.21% variation, indicating that its predictions are highly consistent regardless of which data partition is used for validation. The DecisionTree shows slightly higher variance (0.30-0.31%) but remains very stable. Even the underperforming Ridge classifier exhibits stable—albeit lower—performance across folds. The tight confidence intervals confirm that the reported performance differences are statistically significant and not artifacts of particular data splits. Comparing CV results to test results reveals a generalization gap: Ensemble drops from 95.21% to 91.60% (3.61%), DecisionTree from 94.74% to 91.19% (3.55%), and Ridge from 80.68% to 79.18% (1.50%). The smaller gap for Ridge paradoxically reflects its limited learning capacity—there is less to forget when the model has not captured complex patterns.

figures.caption: Cross-validation performance with error bars
figures.description: Figure 3.4 visualizes cross-validation results with error bars representing standard deviation across the five folds. The tight error bars for all models confirm stable performance regardless of data partitioning. The Ensemble_Bagging shows the smallest error bars, consistent with ensemble methods' theoretical property of reducing variance through averaging. The DecisionTree's slightly larger error bars reflect single-tree sensitivity to training data composition, though the variance remains acceptably low. The consistent gap between non-linear methods (around 95%) and the linear Ridge (around 81%) across all folds confirms that this performance difference is fundamental rather than data-dependent. The figure also illustrates why cross-validation is essential: single train-test splits might produce different rankings due to random variation, but the consistent 5-fold pattern provides confidence in the reported hierarchy.

sections.title: Bias-Variance Decomposition
sections.content_html: Bootstrap-based decomposition (200 iterations) characterized error sources (Geman et al., 1992). Table 3.3 reveals distinct error profiles: Ensemble achieves optimal balance (low bias, low variance); DecisionTree has lowest bias but higher variance; Ridge shows severe underfitting (bias = 0.2276) with minimal variance.

tables.caption: Bias-Variance Decomposition
tables.description: Table 3.3 presents the bias-variance decomposition results from 200 bootstrap iterations. The decomposition reveals fundamentally different error profiles for each model family. The Ensemble_Bagging achieves optimal error composition with 9.66% bias and only 2.55% variance, confirming that bootstrap aggregating successfully reduces prediction variance while maintaining low bias. The DecisionTree shows the lowest bias (8.68%) among all models, indicating that its flexible decision boundaries most accurately capture the true classification function—however, its higher variance (3.31%) reflects sensitivity to training data composition. The Ridge classifier exhibits a dramatically different profile: 22.76% bias dominates its error, while variance is negligible (0.45%). This pattern is characteristic of underfitting—the linear model systematically misclassifies instances because it cannot represent the non-linear decision boundaries required. No amount of additional data or hyperparameter tuning can reduce this bias; it represents a fundamental architectural limitation. The expected loss values (bias + variance) of approximately 10% for non-linear methods versus 23% for Ridge quantify the practical cost of choosing an inappropriate model family.

figures.caption: Stacked bar visualization of bias-variance decomposition
figures.description: Figure 3.5 uses a stacked bar chart to visualize the bias-variance decomposition, with bias shown in one color and variance in another. This visualization immediately reveals the fundamental difference in error composition between model families. For the Ensemble_Bagging and DecisionTree, the bars are similar in total height (around 10%) with variance contributing a modest portion atop a larger bias component. For the Ridge classifier, the bar is dramatically taller (around 23%), almost entirely composed of bias with an imperceptibly thin variance layer. This visual pattern definitively establishes that Ridge's poor performance stems from underfitting rather than overfitting—increasing model complexity or regularization adjustment cannot help because the fundamental problem is insufficient model expressiveness. The visualization also shows how ensemble averaging reduces variance: comparing DecisionTree's variance component to Ensemble's reveals the variance reduction achieved by aggregating 150 trees.

sections.title: Attack Detection Performance
sections.content_html: Table 3.4 presents IDS-specific metrics. Ensemble achieves 87.20% detection rate with only 4.00% false alarms. Ridge detects only 65.36% of attacks (missing over one-third) while generating the highest false alarm rate (7.00%)—unsuitable for security applications.

tables.caption: Attack Detection Performance
tables.description: Table 3.4 presents metrics specifically relevant to intrusion detection system deployment. The Attack Detection Rate (sensitivity/recall for the attack class) measures the proportion of actual attacks correctly identified—critical for security applications where missed attacks can have severe consequences. The Ensemble_Bagging detects 87.20% of attacks, meaning 11,191 of the 12,833 test set attacks are correctly flagged. The DecisionTree achieves similar detection at 86.71%. However, the Ridge classifier detects only 65.36% of attacks—missing 4,445 intrusions that would proceed undetected. The False Alarm Rate measures the proportion of normal connections incorrectly flagged as attacks. The Ensemble's 4.00% false alarm rate means only 388 of 9,711 normal connections trigger alerts, minimizing analyst workload. The Ridge's 7.00% false alarm rate (680 false positives) is 75% higher than Ensemble's, while paradoxically detecting far fewer actual attacks. The Attack Precision values (96.65% for Ensemble, 96.35% for DecisionTree, 92.50% for Ridge) indicate that when these models flag an attack, they are usually correct—but Ridge's lower precision combined with its low detection rate makes it operationally unsuitable.

figures.caption: Detection Rate vs. False Alarm Rate
figures.description: Figure 3.6 plots Detection Rate against False Alarm Rate in a scatter plot format, creating a visual representation of the accuracy-alarm tradeoff for each model. The ideal position is the upper-left corner: high detection rate with low false alarms. The Ensemble_Bagging and DecisionTree both occupy positions in this desirable region, with detection rates above 86% and false alarm rates below 5%. The Ridge classifier appears in a clearly inferior position: lower on the y-axis (worse detection) and further right on the x-axis (more false alarms). This visualization encapsulates the operational reality: deploying the Ridge classifier would result in security teams missing over one-third of attacks while simultaneously handling 75% more false alerts than necessary. The proximity of Ensemble and DecisionTree points suggests either would be acceptable for deployment, with the choice depending on whether the slight accuracy advantage of Ensemble justifies its longer training time.

sections.title: Confusion Matrix Analysis
sections.content_html: Table 3.5 presents confusion matrix values. Ensemble correctly detects 11,191 attacks while missing 1,642; Ridge misses 4,445 attacks—2,803 additional undetected intrusions representing substantial security risk.

tables.caption: Confusion Matrix Values
tables.description: Table 3.5 presents the raw confusion matrix values for each model, revealing the practical implications of performance differences. The Ensemble_Bagging correctly identifies 11,191 of 12,833 attacks (True Positives) while misclassifying only 1,642 attacks as normal (False Negatives) and generating 388 false alerts on normal traffic (False Positives). The DecisionTree produces nearly identical results with 11,127 True Positives, 1,706 False Negatives, and 421 False Positives. The Ridge classifier's confusion matrix tells a concerning story: only 8,388 True Positives means 4,445 attacks go undetected—2,803 more missed attacks than the Ensemble. From a security perspective, these 2,803 additional undetected intrusions could include data breaches, malware installations, or reconnaissance activities that proceed without alerting defenders. Simultaneously, Ridge generates 680 False Positives versus Ensemble's 388—292 additional false alerts that consume analyst attention without security benefit. The True Negative counts (correctly classified normal connections) are relatively similar across models, indicating that differences primarily manifest in attack detection rather than normal traffic classification.

figures.caption: Confusion matrices for all models
figures.description: Figure 3.7 displays confusion matrices for all three models in a side-by-side format using color-coded heatmaps. Darker colors indicate higher values in each cell. The Ensemble and DecisionTree matrices appear nearly identical, with dark cells in the True Positive (upper-left) and True Negative (lower-right) positions, and light cells in the error positions. The Ridge matrix shows a noticeably lighter True Positive cell and darker False Negative cell, visually confirming its attack detection deficiency. The diagonal dominance in the non-linear methods' matrices indicates accurate classification of both classes, while Ridge's off-diagonal activity reveals systematic misclassification. This visualization format allows quick comparison of error patterns: both Ensemble and DecisionTree make similar types of errors in similar proportions, while Ridge exhibits a distinctly different—and less desirable—pattern with disproportionate False Negatives.

sections.title: ROC-AUC Analysis
sections.content_html:
Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) analysis provides threshold-independent evaluation of classifier discrimination ability. Table 3.6 presents Area Under the ROC Curve (AUC) scores with 95% confidence intervals computed via DeLong's method (DeLong et al., 1988).

The Ensemble_Bagging achieves AUC = 0.9642 [0.9612, 0.9672], indicating excellent discrimination between attack and normal traffic across all classification thresholds. The DecisionTree achieves comparable AUC = 0.9589 [0.9556, 0.9622]. The Ridge classifier's AUC = 0.8734 [0.8678, 0.8790] confirms substantially weaker discrimination ability.

Pairwise ROC Comparison: DeLong's test comparing Ensemble vs. Ridge yields z = 24.67 (p < 0.001), confirming statistically significant AUC difference. Ensemble vs. DecisionTree yields z = 2.89 (p = 0.004), indicating modest but significant difference.

Operating Point Analysis: At the default threshold (0.5), Ensemble operates at TPR=0.872, FPR=0.040—near-optimal position on the ROC curve. Adjusting threshold to 0.3 would increase TPR to 0.921 but raise FPR to 0.078, a tradeoff security teams must evaluate based on operational capacity.

tables.caption: ROC-AUC Scores with Confidence Intervals
tables.description: Table 3.6 presents ROC-AUC scores with 95% confidence intervals computed using DeLong's method. AUC values above 0.9 indicate excellent discrimination; 0.8-0.9 indicates good discrimination. Both non-linear methods achieve excellent AUC (>0.95), while Ridge achieves only good discrimination (0.87). The tight confidence intervals (±0.003 to ±0.006) confirm reliable estimates. The 0.09 AUC gap between Ensemble and Ridge quantifies the discrimination penalty of using linear boundaries for this non-linear classification problem.

sections.title: Generalization Analysis
sections.content_html: Table 3.7 shows generalization gap between CV and test performance. Ensemble and DecisionTree show similar gaps (~3.6%), indicating successful learning of generalizable patterns. Ridge's smaller gap (1.5%) reflects limited learning capacity rather than superior generalization.

tables.caption: Generalization Gap Analysis
tables.description: Table 3.6 quantifies the generalization gap—the difference between cross-validation performance (on known attack types) and test set performance (including novel attacks). The Ensemble_Bagging experiences a 3.61 percentage point drop from 95.21% to 91.60%, while the DecisionTree drops 3.55 points from 94.74% to 91.19%. These similar gaps suggest both models learn equally generalizable patterns from the training data. The NSL-KDD test set intentionally includes attack variants absent from training (Tavallaee et al., 2009), so some performance degradation is expected and healthy—it confirms the models are not merely memorizing training examples. The Ridge classifier's smaller gap (1.50 points) might superficially appear favorable, but this interpretation is misleading. Ridge starts from a lower baseline (80.68% CV) and has less room to degrade. More fundamentally, Ridge's limited model capacity means it cannot capture complex patterns from training data in the first place—there is little specialized knowledge to lose when facing novel attacks. The consistent ~3.6% gap for non-linear methods provides a useful expectation for deployment: production performance will likely be several percentage points below cross-validation estimates when novel attack variants appear.

figures.caption: Training vs. test performance comparison
figures.description: Figure 3.8 uses grouped bars to compare cross-validation (training) and test performance for each model. Each model has two adjacent bars—the taller representing CV performance and the shorter representing test performance. The gap between bars visualizes the generalization penalty. For Ensemble and DecisionTree, the bars are both tall with similar gaps, indicating strong performance that degrades modestly when facing novel attacks. For Ridge, both bars are shorter, and the gap is proportionally smaller. This visualization reinforces that Ridge's smaller generalization gap is not a virtue—both its bars are simply lower on the chart. The figure effectively communicates that practitioners should expect approximately 3-4% performance reduction when deploying non-linear models against real-world traffic containing previously unseen attack variants.

figures.caption: Training time comparison
figures.description: Figure 3.9 compares training times across models using a bar chart. The Ensemble_Bagging requires 79.41 seconds—substantially longer than alternatives due to training 150 individual decision trees on bootstrap samples. The DecisionTree completes training in only 0.87 seconds, nearly 100 times faster than the ensemble. The Ridge classifier is fastest at 0.38 seconds, benefiting from its closed-form solution that requires only matrix operations. However, training time should not drive model selection for this problem: all times are under 2 minutes and training is a one-time cost. The critical question is whether the Ensemble's 79-second training investment is justified by its performance advantage. Given the marginal 0.41 percentage point improvement over DecisionTree, practitioners with strict time constraints might reasonably prefer the faster single-tree approach. For production IDS deployment where accuracy is paramount, the ensemble's training time is negligible compared to the operational lifespan of the deployed model.

sections.title: Discussion and Summary
sections.content_html:
Why Ensemble Methods Excel: BaggingClassifier achieves variance reduction through bootstrap aggregating while maintaining low bias (Breiman, 1996). The 150 decision tree estimators provide robust predictions by smoothing individual tree errors.

Decision Tree Competitiveness: The single DecisionTreeClassifier achieves near-equivalent accuracy due to NSL-KDD's well-structured patterns. Trees offer interpretability advantages—analysts can trace decision paths for flagged connections.

Linear Model Limitations: RidgeClassifier's high bias (0.2276) confirms the linear separability assumption fails for intrusion detection. Attack patterns require non-linear decision boundaries that linear models cannot capture.

Key Findings:

  1. Ensemble and tree methods excel (91%+ balanced accuracy, MCC > 0.8)
  2. Linear methods severely underfit (79% balanced accuracy, 0.59 MCC)
  3. Non-linear methods detect 87% of attacks with 4% false alarms vs. Ridge's 65%/7%
  4. All models show ~3.5% generalization gap to novel attacks

Recommendation: Ensemble or tree-based methods are strongly preferred for NSL-KDD classification. Linear methods should only be considered with explicit computational constraints and full awareness of the substantial accuracy penalty.
